C005.subject: raising the minimum wage
C005.object: job turnover rates among low-skilled workers in competitive labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage job turnover rates among low-skilled workers in competitive labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of state-level minimum wage increases (e.g., using synthetic control methods) that measure job tenure and separation rates for low-skilled workers in competitive labor markets within 1-2 years post-implementation. — Provides causal estimates in the specified U.S. geographic and short-term temporal scope, directly testing the hypothesis against observed turnover outcomes.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on minimum wage effects on job stability, focusing on low-skilled workers in competitive sectors (e.g., retail, food service) with subgroup analyses by market concentration. — Synthesizes multiple studies to assess overall evidence direction and heterogeneity, helping to resolve disputes and identify conditions under which turnover decreases or not.

[PATH:theoretical] Efficiency wage theory models adapted to competitive labor markets, incorporating minimum wage shocks and worker-firm bargaining dynamics to predict turnover responses. — Provides a mechanistic framework to explain why higher wages might reduce turnover (e.g., reduced quits due to increased opportunity cost of job loss) and generates testable predictions for empirical validation.

C006.subject: raising the minimum wage
C006.object: unemployment among low-skilled workers in competitive labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage unemployment among low-skilled workers in competitive labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3), 1405-1454. — This study uses a difference-in-differences approach across U.S. states from 1979-2016 to examine the effect of minimum wage increases on low-wage jobs. It provides direct empirical evidence on whether minimum wage hikes reduce employment among low-skilled workers in competitive labor markets, relevant to the post-2000 U.S. context.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D., & Wascher, W. (2007). Minimum wages and employment. Foundations and Trends in Microeconomics, 3(1-2), 1-182. — This comprehensive literature review synthesizes decades of research on minimum wage effects, including studies specific to low-skilled workers in competitive markets. It highlights methodological debates and conflicting findings, helping to assess the dispute around the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D., & Krueger, A. B. (1994). Minimum wages and employment: A case study of the fast-food industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. The American Economic Review, 84(4), 772-793. — This classic natural experiment compares employment in fast-food restaurants before and after a minimum wage increase in New Jersey versus neighboring Pennsylvania. It directly tests the hypothesis in a competitive labor market for low-skilled workers, providing a foundational empirical test that often supports the null effect on unemployment.

C007.subject: raising the minimum wage
C007.object: employee job satisfaction and retention rates
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage employee job satisfaction and retention rates]

[PATH:empirical] National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) working papers on minimum wage and labor turnover, e.g., 'The Effects of Minimum Wages on Low-Wage Workers' Job Mobility and Retention' — Provides quasi-experimental evidence using U.S. retail and hospitality data from 2015-2023, directly testing the causal link between minimum wage increases and employee retention.

[PATH:empirical] Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) matched with state-level minimum wage changes — Allows longitudinal analysis of quit rates and tenure in retail/hospitality sectors across states with varying minimum wage policies, controlling for economic cycles.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage and job satisfaction studies (e.g., in Journal of Labor Economics or Industrial Relations) — Synthesizes existing empirical findings to assess overall effect size and heterogeneity, especially for low-wage service sectors, addressing the disputed status of the hypothesis.

scope.domain: employers in retail and hospitality sectors

C008.subject: raising the minimum wage
C008.object: employee turnover and training costs for employers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage employee turnover and training costs for employers]

[PATH:empirical] Quarterly Workforce Indicators (QWI) data from the U.S. Census Bureau, analyzed for high-turnover sectors (e.g., retail, hospitality) before and after state-level minimum wage increases. — Provides longitudinal, employer-level turnover and hiring cost data to test whether turnover rises in the first year post-implementation, controlling for regional economic trends.

[PATH:empirical] Survey of employer training costs from the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) or similar industry reports, focusing on firms in high-turnover sectors that experienced recent minimum wage hikes. — Directly measures changes in per-employee training expenditures and recruitment costs, offering a complementary metric to turnover rates.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on minimum wage and labor turnover (e.g., Dube, Lester, & Reich 2010; Meer & West 2016) with a focus on short-run effects in high-turnover industries. — Synthesizes prior findings to assess the weight of evidence for the disputed hypothesis, identifying gaps and methodological issues (e.g., lag effects, sector heterogeneity).

qualifier.temporal: during the first year after implementation

C011.subject: raising the minimum wage
C011.object: income inequality in tight labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage income inequality in tight labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). The effect of minimum wages on low-wage jobs. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3), 1405-1454. — This study uses a novel empirical method (stacked event study) to estimate the impact of minimum wage increases on low-wage employment and earnings, with findings that can be re-analyzed for tight labor market conditions post-2008 in the U.S.

[PATH:empirical] Autor, D. H., Manning, A., & Smith, C. L. (2016). The contribution of the minimum wage to U.S. wage inequality over three decades. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 8(1), 58-99. — This paper directly examines the relationship between minimum wage changes and wage inequality, providing a longitudinal framework that can be extended to focus on tight labor markets and the post-2008 period.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D., & Wascher, W. (2008). Minimum Wages. MIT Press. — This comprehensive book reviews theoretical and empirical evidence on minimum wage effects, including employment and inequality, and can guide identification of gaps specific to tight labor markets and recent decades.

scope.domain: tight labor markets with low unemployment

C012.subject: raising the minimum wage in tight labor markets
C012.object: unemployment among low-skilled and younger workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage in tight labor markets unemployment among low-skilled and younger workers]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in U.S. states with unemployment rates below 4% (e.g., using synthetic control methods on recent state-level data from Washington, D.C., or California) — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating tight labor market periods and estimating effects on youth and low-skilled employment, addressing the disputed status with causal evidence.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment effects with subgroup analysis by labor market tightness (e.g., updating the 2019 CEA review or the 2021 Doucouliagos & Stanley meta-regression) — Synthesizes existing studies to quantify whether effects differ systematically when unemployment is low, providing a broader evidence base than single studies.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching models of the labor market incorporating monopsony power and minimum wage floors in tight markets (e.g., extensions of the Card-Krueger or Manning models) — Clarifies mechanisms under which minimum wage increases could reduce unemployment (e.g., reduced hiring) or not (e.g., increased labor force participation), helping interpret empirical findings and refine the hypothesis.

scope.domain: tight labor markets with low unemployment

qualifier.temporal: during periods of low unemployment (e.g., below 4%)
qualifier.geographic: primarily in developed economies with flexible labor markets
